pools.title: The Comparative Range: Minds Built Nothing Alike
pools.covers: reading §0.1 (claims C2, C3, C4, C7, C12, C14) incl. tbl-same-feats; lecture 0 slides gallery_everyday, gallery_child, gallery_animals, gallery_machines, twenty_watts, the_theme

items.stem: A person, a honeybee, an octopus, and a protein-folding program all do things we are willing to call intelligent, yet the four share almost nothing in what they are physically made of. What does the chapter draw from that fact?

options.text: Whatever explains intelligent behavior cannot be only a fact about the material a system is made of.
options.why: Correct. The argument turns on a mismatch: the behavior is shared and the physical makeup is not, so the explanation has to be pitched somewhere above the level of tissue and silicon. Finding a description that floats free of the material is what the chapter says the field exists to do.

options.text: Intelligent behavior arises only where neurons are present, so the machine cases merely resemble the real thing.
options.why: This is the position the machine examples are chosen to unsettle. The chapter stops short of claiming the programs have minds, but it treats their behavior as real enough that an account resting on neurons alone has a problem to answer.

options.text: Because the four systems differ so sharply, no single science can hold them in view at once.
options.why: This inverts the chapter's conclusion. The diversity is precisely why a description above the level of physical makeup is wanted, and supplying one is what lets a single field study all four side by side.

options.text: The shared behavior points back to a common ancestor whose nervous system all four inherited.
options.why: Common descent does explain shared traits among related organisms, but it cannot reach a protein-folding program, and the chapter's claim concerns the level a description is pitched at rather than lineage.

items.stem: A classmate argues that a program that taught itself to beat the strongest human Go players is not really intelligent, because there are no neurons anywhere in it. Which reply best matches the position the course actually takes?

options.text: The course does not claim the program has a mind, but its behavior troubles any account resting on neurons alone.
options.why: Correct. The claim made about the machine cases is deliberately narrow, and the lecture flags the narrowness out loud: whether such systems have minds is left open as one of the questions the course will work on, while the argument that physical makeup cannot be the whole explanation is treated as hard to dodge.

options.text: The course holds that the Go program has a mind in the same sense a person does, since it solves a hard problem.
options.why: This overclaims in the direction the course is careful to avoid. Solving a hard problem is offered as evidence about what explains intelligent behavior, not as a settled verdict about which systems have minds.

options.text: The course agrees with the classmate: neurons are what make a system intelligent, so machine performance is a separate topic.
options.why: Treating the machine cases as a topic apart is what the course refuses to do. Artificial systems are set up on day one as a running comparison rather than as a category held away from living minds.

options.text: The course sets the question aside as unanswerable, since nobody has directly observed a mind other than their own.
options.why: The difficulty of studying minds from the outside is a real problem the chapter names among the field's driving questions, but naming it is not the same as declining to compare cases, which the chapter does throughout.

items.stem: The lecture showed spectrograms of HOT, HAT, HIT and HEAD spoken by two people. The same word from two speakers looked nothing alike, while different words from a single speaker sometimes looked more similar to each other. What does that finding show about recognizing a spoken word?

options.text: The category the listener recovers is not sitting in the sound as a stable pattern, so the listener must supply it.
options.why: Correct. This is why the demonstration was chosen. If the sound itself carried a reliable signature for HOT, recognition would be a matter of matching; because it does not, recognition has to be something the listener's own machinery constructs.

options.text: Listeners depend on surrounding context rather than the sound, so a word heard in isolation cannot be identified.
options.why: Context certainly helps, but the chapter's companion example cuts against this reading: a single syllable of "hello" from a familiar voice is enough to identify the speaker, with no context at all.

options.text: Spectrograms are too coarse an instrument to display the acoustic features that actually distinguish one vowel from another.
options.why: This blames the instrument for what the demonstration was built to reveal. The variability shown is a genuine property of speech, and it is the reason speech recognition was hard for engineers for so long.

options.text: Speakers unconsciously converge on a shared acoustic target for each word, which is what makes their speech intelligible.
options.why: Convergence of this kind would predict that the same word looks alike across speakers, which is exactly the prediction the spectrograms falsify.

items.stem: Among the animal cases the chapter presents, what is distinctive about the octopus?

options.text: Most of its neurons are threaded through its arms rather than gathered into a central brain.
options.why: Correct. The organization is what makes the case interesting: an octopus solving a problem raises the question of what exactly is doing the solving, since its nervous system is distributed rather than centralized.

options.text: Its whole nervous system holds fewer than a million neurons, far fewer than the task appears to need.
options.why: That description belongs to the honeybee, whose brain the chapter compares to a grain of rice, and whose waggle dance it treats as the striking feat.

options.text: It navigates tens of thousands of miles each year to reach places it has never previously visited.
options.why: Long-distance navigation to unfamiliar feeding grounds is the Arctic tern's feat rather than the octopus's.

options.text: It performs its most impressive feats with no neurons involved in the process at all.
options.why: Having no neurons whatsoever is what sets the artificial systems apart, and it is the basis of the chapter's sharpest version of its argument.

items.stem: The chapter sets the roughly twenty watts a human brain runs on against the power drawn by the machines that fold proteins or master Go. What is that contrast offered to establish?

options.text: A brain achieves feats of this kind on a small fraction of the energy the matching machines require.
options.why: Correct. The comparison is there to make the brain strange again. Eighty-six billion neurons, each in conversation with thousands of others, produce all of this on less power than a household lightbulb, while the machines that rival it on single tasks draw the electricity of a small town.

options.text: Energy efficiency is the property separating a genuine mind from a system that merely imitates one.
options.why: Efficiency is presented as a puzzle worth explaining rather than as a criterion for having a mind, and the chapter is careful not to offer any such criterion this early.

options.text: The brain's low power budget is why it works more slowly than a machine on tasks of similar difficulty.
options.why: No trade-off of this sort is claimed. The point is the opposite one: the brain manages a far wider range of tasks without paying the energy cost the machines pay.

options.text: Machines will match the brain's abilities once their power consumption has been brought down far enough.
options.why: This turns a comparison into a prediction the chapter never makes. Where the machines fall short is treated as an open question rather than as a matter of available electricity.

items.stem: According to the chapter, what makes it remarkable that most young children master the grammar of their native language within a few years?

options.text: They manage it from nothing but the talk around them, with no lessons, no rules, and no correction.
options.why: Correct. The absence of instruction is the whole force of the example. Decades of expensive engineering effort have gone into the same problem, and a small child solves it from ordinary overheard conversation.

options.text: They manage it before the brain regions supporting language have finished developing physically.
options.why: Claims about the maturation of particular brain regions are not what this example rests on, and the chapter makes no argument here about developmental timing in the brain.

options.text: They manage it despite hearing speech that adults have simplified into an incomplete version of the grammar.
options.why: Simplified speech to children is a real phenomenon, but treating it as an obstacle reverses the usual argument, and the chapter's point rests on the absence of teaching rather than the quality of the input.

options.text: They manage it in whatever language surrounds them, which adults learning a second language can no longer do.
options.why: The comparison with adult second-language learning is a genuine topic elsewhere, but the feat highlighted here is learning a first grammar without instruction of any kind.

items.stem: A commentator writes: "A new system composes music that moves people, just as human composers do. That proves the human brain must work the same way this system does." Where does the reasoning go wrong by the chapter's lights?

options.text: Shared behavior across unlike systems shows the material cannot be the whole story, not that mechanisms match.
options.why: Correct. The chapter's argument runs from shared behavior to a constraint on what an explanation must look like. Reading it as an identity claim about mechanisms gets it backwards, since the same behavior turning up in a bee, an octopus and a machine is evidence that very different mechanisms can produce it.

options.text: Music is an aesthetic matter rather than a cognitive one, so the case falls outside what the field actually studies.
options.why: The field's scope is drawn much more widely than this, and the chapter treats capacities from navigation to humor to protein folding as fair game.

options.text: Machines cannot move people emotionally, so the premise fails before the conclusion is even reached.
options.why: Whether the effect is genuine is not the flaw being probed here, and the chapter is willing to grant that artificial systems produce apt and impressive results.

options.text: Nothing follows from one case, and the argument would go through if enough composing systems were compared.
options.why: Adding cases would not repair it. The problem is the shape of the inference rather than the size of the sample, since more matches would still not show that the mechanisms are the same.

items.stem: In lecture, a picture of sliced oranges was shown, and some students noticed they had become a little hungry. The lecture flagged this as a preview of a deep question. Which question was it?

options.text: Why identifying an object should come bundled with wanting it, rather than the two being separate matters.
options.why: Correct. Recognition arriving already tied to an appraisal is a real puzzle about what minds are for, and the course takes it up directly when it reaches how nervous systems work out whether something is good or bad.

options.text: Why a picture of an object produces much the same bodily response that the object itself would produce.
options.why: Responses to depictions are an interesting topic in their own right, but the puzzle raised was about recognition and wanting arriving together rather than about pictures standing in for objects.

options.text: Why some categories of object are recognized faster than others when they are seen only briefly.
options.why: Differences in recognition speed across categories belong to the study of pattern recognition, which the course reaches much later and for different reasons.

options.text: Why people can recognize an object from a photograph they have never seen before, or from an angle they have not seen.
options.why: Generalizing to a never-before-seen instance is a genuine puzzle the course takes up, and the spectrogram demonstration in the same lecture makes the point for speech.

items.stem: The chapter opens by pointing out that its first sentence has in all likelihood never been produced before, and yet the reader understands it effortlessly. What does that observation establish?

options.text: Understanding cannot work by retrieving a stored meaning, since a novel sentence has none to retrieve.
options.why: Correct. Novelty is what rules out the simplest account. Whatever the reader is doing has to build a meaning from an arrangement encountered for the first time, which is a far harder thing than looking one up.

options.text: Understanding depends on the reader having encountered every individual word in the sentence before.
options.why: Familiar words are necessary but nowhere near sufficient, and the observation is aimed at the arrangement rather than at the vocabulary.

options.text: Written language is processed differently from speech, since only writing produces genuinely novel sentences.
options.why: Novelty is a property of ordinary speech as much as of writing, and the chapter treats ink marks and air vibrations in the same breath as two routes to the same accomplishment.

options.text: Comprehension is slower for unfamiliar sentences, which is why careful reading takes deliberate effort.
options.why: The striking thing about the example is the absence of effort, and the chapter emphasizes that the reader takes the sentence in with no sense of working at it.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain why the range of cases in this module — a person, a honeybee, an octopus, and a program with no neurons at all — makes trouble for any explanation of intelligence pitched at the level of what a system is physically made of. Say what kind of description the chapter proposes reaching for instead.
items.answer: Each of these systems does something we are willing to call intelligent: a person understands a sentence never spoken before, a bee communicates the direction and distance of flowers, an octopus works out a jar, a program predicts how a protein folds. But they are made of almost nothing in common — three pounds of tissue, a brain the size of a grain of rice, neurons distributed through eight arms, and silicon. So an explanation given in terms of the material cannot cover all four, because there is no shared material to appeal to. What the chapter proposes instead is a description of what a mind is doing that floats free of what it is made of, pitched at the level of information and process rather than tissue. That is the description the field calls computational, and having one is what makes it possible to study these cases side by side as instances of a single subject.
rubric: Names at least two of the cases and says, for each, what it does that counts as intelligent.
States plainly that the systems share almost nothing physically.
Draws the conclusion that an explanation in terms of physical makeup cannot cover all the cases at once.
Says the alternative is a description pitched above the material, in terms of information and process.
Connects that description to why one field can study these cases together.

items.stem: The chapter's table of four systems that do intelligent things counts neurons for the human, the bee and the octopus, but measures the AI model in parameters and its appetite as "a warehouse of computers" — and leaves the bee's and the octopus's power cells blank. What does the table's refusal to fill every cell with a comparable number show?

options.text: The systems differ so deeply that even the units of measurement do not carry across from one to the next.
options.why: Correct. The blanks are the honest part. No power figure exists for a nervous system on its own, and parameters are not neurons under another name. When the yardsticks themselves fail to line up, the claim that these systems share almost nothing lands harder than any list of differing numbers would.

options.text: Measurements of invertebrate nervous systems are unreliable, so the chapter withholds the figures it cannot properly trust.
options.why: Reliability is not the issue: the table does give counts for both the bee and the octopus, and its sourcing record traces each to a published study. What it omits is power, which nobody has measured for a nervous system alone.

options.text: The chapter treats artificial systems as a separate category that its comparison is not really meant to include.
options.why: Artificial systems are the opposite of excluded. The argument needs a case with no neurons at all, and the table's last row is exactly where that case sits.

options.text: Neuron counts predict capability poorly, so the chapter avoids implying that more neurons would mean more intelligence.
options.why: Whether counts predict capability is a real question, and one the octopus quietly complicates, but the blanks are about measurements nobody has made rather than about an inference the chapter declines to draw.

items.stem: A student objects that the opening feats — understanding a sentence nobody has spoken before, knowing a friend from a single "hello" — cannot really be hard, since we do them constantly and without noticing. How does the chapter answer that?

options.text: Performing a thing endlessly and without effort is why its difficulty goes unnoticed, and is no evidence that it is easy.
options.why: Correct. The chapter separates two things that ordinarily travel together: how hard a problem is, and how hard it feels. These feats outran the best engineering for most of human history while costing an ordinary person nothing, and that gap is where the field lives.

options.text: The feats are easy for people and hard for machines, so how hard something is depends on what kind of system attempts it.
options.why: This makes difficulty relative to the system, which runs against the chapter's point. The problems are hard in their own right, and it is the human case that stands in need of explaining.

options.text: They only feel effortless through practice, and any sufficiently practised skill eventually becomes automatic.
options.why: Practice does automatize skills, but the chapter's lead example is understanding a sentence that has never been produced before, which nobody can have practised.

options.text: Each feat is fairly simple on its own and seems impressive only when many of them are listed together.
options.why: The chapter dwells on single cases — one syllable, one sentence — precisely because each is meant to be remarkable alone rather than by accumulation.

items.stem: Having set the human, animal and machine feats side by side, the chapter says the two smallest and hardest questions to ask are how? and why? What does asking both, rather than either one, commit the field to?

options.text: An account that says by what means an ability works still owes a separate answer about what the ability is there for.
options.why: Correct. The two questions come apart: a complete story about the machinery leaves the question of what the machinery is for untouched, and a good answer about purpose explains nothing about mechanism. The course is built on keeping both open at once.

options.text: An account of the mechanism, once complete, will contain the answer about purpose as one of its consequences.
options.why: This collapses the pair into one question, which is the move the chapter is guarding against by naming two.

options.text: An account must choose between the two, since a mechanistic answer and a purposive one cannot both be correct.
options.why: Neither question is offered as ruling out the other; the chapter treats them as two things to ask about one system.

options.text: An account of purpose has to come first, because a mechanism cannot be described until its goal is known.
options.why: No priority of that kind is claimed here, and the chapter asks both questions of every case without ordering them.

items.stem: The opening section closes by asking whether brain and cognitive science is "really one subject, or a loose collection of older disciplines that only happen to overlap." What is the standing of that question at this point?

options.text: Genuinely open, and deliberately left unsettled here rather than answered.
options.why: Correct. The chapter raises the doubt about its own field on purpose and hands it forward. Taking a position on it is the work of the section that follows, and the answer there is careful rather than reassuring.

options.text: Rhetorical: the chapter has just demonstrated the field's unity and is inviting the reader to agree.
options.why: Nothing before this point argues for unity. What has been shown is a range of systems and a range of researchers, which is what makes the question worth asking.

options.text: Settled in the negative: the chapter's considered position is that these remain separate disciplines with no real unity.
options.why: The chapter is honest about how disconnected the disciplines are, but it treats their unity as a wager worth making rather than one already lost.

options.text: A matter of academic administration rather than a substantive question about the subject.
options.why: The question is substantive for this book, since whether these inquiries are facets of one subject is what would justify studying them together at all.

items.stem: What is brain and cognitive science, as this book uses the term?

options.text: The interdisciplinary, computational study of the mind and brain, pursued across humans, other animals and machines.
options.why: Correct. Both adjectives carry weight. Interdisciplinary, because no one field's tools reach everything that shapes a mind; computational, because that is the description that fits a person, a bee and a machine at once.

options.text: The branch of neuroscience that works out how particular brain structures give rise to thought and behavior.
options.why: This describes roughly what neuroscience contributes, which the book treats as one discipline among several rather than as the whole enterprise.

options.text: The engineering discipline concerned with building machines that reproduce human reasoning and perception.
options.why: That is close to artificial intelligence, which the book counts as one of the contributing fields and as a source of comparisons.

options.text: The philosophical study of how mental states are related to physical states of the body.
options.why: The mind–body relation is a question the book takes up, and philosophy is one of the disciplines it draws on, but neither is the field as a whole.

items.stem: Which term does this book use for the interdisciplinary, computational study of the mind — the enterprise that gathers the questions asked about human, animal and artificial minds under one name?

options.text: brain and cognitive science
options.why: Correct. The name is doing work the book is explicit about: it gathers questions that grew up in separate disciplines, and asserts that they are questions about one subject.

options.text: cognitive psychology
options.why: One of the contributing disciplines, and the one asking what operations the mind performs — a part of the enterprise rather than the whole of it.

options.text: artificial intelligence
options.why: Another contributing discipline, and a running source of comparisons, but the book keeps it as one lens among several.

options.text: levels of analysis
options.why: The frame that sorts the field's questions into kinds. It organizes the enterprise; it is not a name for it.

items.stem: The chapter claims that our own cognitive feats go unnoticed because they are performed constantly and without effort, not because they are simple. In a short paragraph, explain the distinction being drawn, and say why the chapter chooses to open on ordinary experience rather than on a laboratory finding.
items.answer: The chapter separates how hard a problem actually is from how hard it feels to the person solving it. Understanding a sentence, recognizing a voice, and reading a scene are all effortless from the inside, and that effortlessness is exactly what hides their difficulty — we notice the things we struggle with, so a capacity that never fails never draws attention. The evidence that these are hard problems comes from elsewhere: they defeated the best engineering for most of human history, and some of them are still not reliably solved. Opening on ordinary experience puts the reader's own mind in the position of the thing to be explained, which a laboratory result could not do. It also makes the field's central puzzle available before any technical vocabulary has been introduced, so the reader feels the question before being handed the machinery for answering it.
rubric: Distinguishes the difficulty of a problem from the felt effort of solving it.
Says that constancy and effortlessness are what conceal the difficulty, rather than evidence of simplicity.
Gives at least one of the chapter's examples of an effortless-but-hard feat.
Points to evidence of difficulty from outside introspection — that these problems resisted engineering, or remain unsolved.
Gives a reason for opening on the reader's own experience: it makes the reader the case to be explained, or raises the puzzle before any vocabulary exists for it.
